column4: ### Defining Faith
column5: ### Definition of Faith

column4: Faith is a commonly misunderstood and misrepresented aspect of Christianity. As the saying goes, “there is a ditch on both sides of the road”! Because the word faith is so commonly used without proper explanation in our modern Christianity, it can come to pick up erroneous definitions amplified through misunderstanding. Faith is often portrayed either as a blanketed statement of abstracted belief or as an almost mystical power or “magic,” something you possess in a specific measured and limited amount.
column5: Faith is an aspect of Christianity that is commonly misunderstood and misrepresented. As the saying goes, “There is a ditch on both sides of the road”! Because in much of contemporary Christianity the word faith is often used without proper clarification, it takes on distorted meanings further fueled by misunderstanding. Faith is often presented either as a blanket statement of abstract belief or as an almost mystical force or “magic”, that is, something you possess in a specific, measured, and limited quantity.

column4: #### What Faith is Not
column5: #### What Faith Is Not

column4: Faith misrepresented abstractly has no specific conviction or persuasion. This is often evident with a bit of probing as this representation of faith cannot be made specific. If you ask, ‘what do you believe’ or ‘why do you believe’ the person with this understanding of faith often cannot clarify beyond ‘I believe’. 1 Peter 3:15 says we should be ready to give an answer for the hope that is in us.
column5: Presenting faith abstractly does not indicate any specific belief or persuasion. A little scrutiny usually makes this evident, because this representation of faith cannot be made specific. If you ask, ‘What do you have faith in?’ or ‘Why do you have faith?’ the person holding this understanding often cannot explain beyond, ‘I have faith.’ 1 Peter 3:15 says that we should be ready to give an answer concerning the hope that is in us.

column4: Sometimes people think of faith like a magical power-but that’s not what Scripture teaches. Faith is about a real relationship built on trust. In Scripture, faith is far more dynamic and relational-it’s rooted in persuasion, trust, and confidence in God’s character and promises. It’s not an impersonal force but an engaged response to God that shapes thoughts, feelings, and actions.
column5: Sometimes people think of faith as a magical force-but Scripture does not teach that. Faith is about a real relationship based on trust. column4: #### Faith is Persuasion
column5: #### Faith Is Being Persuaded

column4: So, what is faith? Persuasion! The Greek word ***pistis*** means persuasion, or the result of being persuaded. We are to have persuasion towards God. In English we might say faith (persuasion) ‘**in** God’. If you are married, you hopefully have faith ‘**in’** your spouse. You believe that they will do what they said they would do, and you believe that they are being authentic and genuine. This trust should extend beyond what they’ve said, to extend to them in general.
column5: So, what is faith? Persuasion! The Greek word ***pistis*** means persuasion, or the result of being persuaded. We are to have persuasion about God. In English we can say faith (persuasion) ‘**in** God’. If you are married, hopefully you have faith ‘**in’** your spouse. You believe that they will do what they said they would do, and you believe that they are genuine and real. This trust ought to extend beyond the things they have said, to their person in general.

column4: Developing faith, persuasion, and trust in a relationship takes time and experience. Hopefully in life you have learned how to develop a trusting relationship with another person. The principles you’ve learned that allow you to increase your trust in someone you know will also allow you can increase your faith in God. Faith in a relationship is increased over time, in experience, with consistency, and through small and large actions that build your confidence in the other person’s character and nature.

column4: ‘Faith towards God’, is relational. Relationships are built by two parties, not one. The good news about our faith in God is that God is responsible for His side of the relationship (made possible by the atoning death of Jesus, and the infilling of His spirit at rebirth), and He helps us on our side too (through the work of the Comforter - the Holy Spirit). God is doing almost all the work, our part (as we will discuss later in this chapter) is to walk *WITH* Him in obedience.

God is doing almost all the work; our part (as we will describe later in this chapter) is to walk *with* Him in obedience.

column4: ### Jesus Matures Our Faith
column5: ### Jesus perfects our faith

column4: Jesus is the author and perfecter of our faith (Hebrews 12:2). Our faith is designed to be continually growing and expanding. We don’t reach a single point where we have enough ‘faith’, but rather our faith increases. Consider a deep and personal relationship you have in your life today. As in any relationship we don't arrive at a specific milestone where now we ‘know’ the person. We continue to know them, and increase our knowledge of them, and this refines, shapes, and grows our relationship.

column4: There are two Greek words for ‘Word’ in the Bible-**logos** and **rhema**. Understanding the difference helps us see how faith grows.
column5: There are two Greek words for ‘word’ in the Bible-**logos** and **rhema**. Understanding the difference shows us how faith grows.

column4: **Logos**: generally, refers to the **concept, idea, reason, or broader expression of God’s word**. It encompasses a universal, foundational truth or message and is often used to describe God’s eternal wisdom and Christ Himself as the living Word.
column5: **Logos**: Generally refers to the concept, idea, reason, or broader expression of God’s Word. It encompasses a universal, foundational truth or message and is often used to describe God’s eternal wisdom and Christ Himself as the living Word.

column4: **Rhema (G4487)**: emphasizes a **specific, spoken word or utterance**. It typically refers to a particular word or message given in a specific moment, especially a spoken or revealed word that applies directly to a person’s situation.
column5: **Rhema (G4487)**: emphasizes a **specific, spoken word or phrase**. It generally points to a particular word or message given at a specific moment, especially spoken or revealed speech that applies directly to a person’s condition.

column4: *Logos* is like the entire message of a book, whereas *rhema* is like a particular passage or sentence that speaks directly to someone at a given moment. While *logos* is God’s overarching truth, *rhema* is when part of that truth is spoken to an individual in a personal, applicable way. Together, they illustrate the fullness of God’s communication: *logos* as the broad, foundational truths of God’s character and will, and *rhema* as the specific, applied word that brings that truth alive in a person’s life and situation.
column5: *Logos* is like the entire message of a book, whereas *Rhema* is like a specific passage or sentence that speaks directly to someone at a particular moment. While *Logos* is God’s all-encompassing truth, *Rhema* is when a portion of that same truth is spoken to an individual in a personal and applicable way. Together they highlight the perfection of God’s communication: *Logos* as the broad, foundational realities of God’s character and will, and *Rhema* as the specific, applied word that brings that truth to life in a person’s situation and condition.

column4: ### Example of a Rhema Word in Action
column5: ### An example of a Rhema word in action

column4: God promises revelation and wisdom for all those that ask. When He speaks to us, that utterance is a *rhema* word. Rhema words are from God and serve to confirm, lead, and guide us. They are not a replacement for the *logos* word, nor do they carry authority of scripture. *Rhema* words are to be judged by the same standard as prophecy or interpretation of tongues (see the chapter on the Holy Spirit for an in-depth study on this topic).

column4: Jesus goes on to say, ‘*blessed are they who have not seen and have believe*d’. This is not Jesus encouraging ‘blind or ignorant faith’ or rejecting the use of empirical evidence. But He is saying that we are more blessed when we can believe without the need for empirical proof. Why? If our faith, our trust, was limited to purely what we had seen empirically demonstrated, we could never have any confidence in the future work. We would have great confidence in what had been accomplished but would not walk in the peace of God for our tomorrows and for our future.
column5: Jesus goes on to say, ‘*Blessed are those who have believed without seeing*’. This is not Jesus encouraging ‘blind or ignorant faith’ or a dismissal of using experiential testimony. Rather, He is saying that we are more blessed when we can believe without experiential proof. Why? If our faith—our trust—were limited only to the things we have seen empirically proven, we would never have confidence about what is yet to be done. We would have great confidence in what had already happened, but we would not walk in God’s peace for our tomorrow and our future.
